turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I... I didn't exactly want to come in, to be honest. My wife suggested it. Actually, she insisted on it. But I suppose I'm here because things have just been... confusing lately. I mean, I'm a teaching assistant, I'm used to analyzing texts, looking for subtext, reading between the lines—it's what I do. And for the past year, I've been noticing these... patterns. 

My wife, she works in a corporate office, and she's been having these late meetings. And I know, I know, she says it's just normal office stuff, end-of-quarter push, new project deadlines, that sort of thing. But then there are these little changes in her work messages, the ones she sends me during the day. Just slight shifts in phrasing, or the timing of them. And when you lay it all out—the late meetings, the specific words she uses, the exact time she sends a text—they line up too precisely to feel accidental. It's not just a coincidence. It feels... it feels like there’s a private signal in them, you know? Like they're meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. I’ve tried to explain this to her, how the probability of all these things aligning perfectly is just astronomically low, but she just gets frustrated and tells me I'm overthinking it. But I'm not overthinking it, I'm just observing what's right in front of me.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe these messages are definitely sending you a hidden signal, or is it possible you might be mistaken?
turns.patient_response:
Mistaken? Well, I mean... look, as an academic, as someone who literally spends his days grading undergraduate papers on textual analysis, I am always open to the *concept* of being mistaken. Falsifiability is the cornerstone of any sound theory, right? So, naturally, when this all started about a year ago, my first thought was exactly that. I told myself, 'Okay, maybe I'm just reading too much into this.' I tried to dismiss it. I really, really did. 

But then you have to actually look at the data. I know my wife says the late meetings and these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but you have to understand the sheer statistical improbability of it all. If she has a late meeting on a Tuesday, for example, the message I get at exactly 3:15 PM will always, *always* use the word 'regret' instead of 'sorry.' 'I regret I'll be late' instead of 'Sorry, running late.' And it's been happening consistently for the past year. A full year! You don't just accidentally swap syntax like that with perfect chronological correlation. It’s too precise. It’s mathematically too precisely aligned to feel accidental. 

So, to answer your question, no, I really don't think I'm mistaken. Because when you put it all together—the late meetings, the structural shifts in her texts, the timing—it forms a complete, intentional narrative. There is absolutely a private signal in them. It's a deliberate, constructed signal meant to tell me something she won't say directly to my face. I just... I haven't fully decoded the ultimate meaning of it yet, but the existence of the signal itself is undeniable. I mean, if you saw the notes I started keeping just to track the timestamps and the vocabulary shifts, you'd see exactly what I mean. It's all right there. You can't just ignore a pattern once it reveals itself like that, you know? It would be intellectually dishonest of me to just pretend it's a coincidence.

I'm talking about empirical evidence. Things that are actually there in the physical world. The text messages exist on my phone. You could look at them yourself. The timestamps are real. The words she uses are real words that she actually typed. I'm just reading them. I'm analyzing the data that is objectively present. 

It's not about seeing things that aren't there; it's about seeing the connections between the things that *are* there. Which is exactly what I try to explain to my students when we're doing close readings of, say, a modernist novel. You don't just look at the surface plot; you look at the recurring motifs, the syntactical choices, the structural anomalies. If an author uses a specific, unusual word three times in a single chapter, you don't just say, 'Oh, they must have liked that word today.' You ask *why*. You look at the context. You look at the pattern. 

And that's all I'm doing here. I'm just applying basic analytical rigor to my own life. Because when the data points align with such startling precision—like the 'regret' versus 'sorry' dichotomy I mentioned, which, by the way, only ever happens on Tuesdays and Thursdays, never Mondays or Wednesdays—you have to acknowledge it. But no, to answer your question directly, I don't hallucinate. I just pay very, very close attention to the reality that's right in front of me. Probably closer attention than most people bother to pay, to be perfectly honest. People are so quick to dismiss things as coincidence because it's easier, isn't it? It's intellectually lazy, but it's easier. But I can't do that. I just can't turn off that analytical part of my brain when the evidence is so glaringly obvious.
